862.title: The North American martyrs (1640s)
862.hook: Jesuits and lay helpers killed in the Great Lakes region, remembered with the harm of colonization
862.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States and Canada keep a feast of the North American martyrs, with shrines in New York and in Ontario, and some dioceses now pair it with prayer and education about Indigenous history.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kateri Tekakwitha, scarred by smallpox, who walked to a mission near Montreal. Your line was lily of the mohawks. Today's story happened in those same forests.

A French priest with mutilated hands kneels before an altar in France. His captors had cut and chewed his fingers, and the rules of the time said a priest's hands had to be whole to say Mass. Tradition says the pope gave him permission anyway. Then he did something hard to understand. He went back across the ocean, to the country where he had been tortured, and he was killed there. His name was Isaac Jogues, one of a group the Church calls the North American martyrs.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH MUTILATED HANDS.` → `PERMISSION TO SAY MASS.` → `HE WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. Jesuit priests, among them Jean de Brébeuf and Isaac Jogues, and lay helpers like René Goupil and Jean de Lalande, who worked among the Wendat people, sometimes called the Huron, around the Great Lakes. They learned the languages, lived in the villages, wrote reports home. Brébeuf is remembered for a Christmas song in the Wendat language. Second, how they died. The Wendat and the Haudenosaunee nations, including the Mohawk, were at war, and the French were allied with the Wendat. The missionaries died in that war: some killed in raids, others tortured and killed after capture. Jogues wrote that Goupil was killed for making the sign of the cross over a child. Catholics honor them as martyrs, who died for the faith they carried and would not abandon their missions. Jesus says it in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Third, the rest of the story. The missions came with European contact, and with it diseases that emptied Native villages. Some Wendat blamed the missionaries. The missions were tied to a French colonial project that, over time, took land and power from Native nations. The Haudenosaunee weren't villains in a saint's story; they were nations with their own reasons, alliances and dead. Fourth, holding both. Some Catholics in North America now speak of these martyrs alongside an honest account of colonization. Courage and harm sit in the same story. Remembering one alone would be untrue.
screen: `PRIESTS AND LAY HELPERS.` · `KILLED IN A WAR OF NATIONS.` · `DISEASE, LAND AND POWER.` · `COURAGE AND HARM TOGETHER.` · then, large: `LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: In one hand, hold the missionaries: their courage, their love for the people they lived among, their deaths. In the other, hold the Native nations: the sickness that emptied their villages, the land taken, the wars made worse by powers from across the sea, and notice which hand wants to drop. If you pray, pray for the dead on every side; if not, hold them all, without choosing.
Isaac Jogues. A Jesuit priest tortured and mutilated among the Wendat, who returned to the same country and was killed there, one of the North American martyrs.
Your line: remember all of it. The truest telling keeps everyone in the room. Day eight hundred sixty-two.

863.title: Francis de Sales (1567–1622)
863.hook: a gentle bishop who taught that everyone can be devout, in any job
863.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Francis de Sales, and his Introduction to the Devout Life is still read by laypeople; Salesian religious orders carry his name, and Catholic writers and journalists keep him as their patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the North American martyrs, among them Isaac Jogues, held together with the harm of colonization. Your line was remember all of it.

Doors stay shut. A young priest has been sent into a region of the Alps where the people had become Protestant, and nobody wants to hear him preach. Some days he gets no audience at all. So he writes short leaflets explaining the Catholic faith plainly, and tradition says he slipped them under doors. The Church now calls him a patron of writers and journalists. He would become a bishop known less for winning arguments than for his gentleness. Today, Francis de Sales.
screen: `DOORS STAY SHUT.` → `LEAFLETS UNDER DOORS.` → `A PATRON OF WRITERS.`

segments.voice: First, a bishop without his city. Francis was named bishop of Geneva, but Geneva was a Calvinist city, so he lived and worked in nearby Annecy. He preached, heard confessions and answered piles of letters from people trying to live their faith. Second, a book for everyone. Out of those letters came his Introduction to the Devout Life, addressed to a reader he calls Philothea, a name meaning one who loves God. His point: devotion isn't only for monks and nuns. It must fit the life you actually have. A soldier, a shopkeeper, a servant, a married woman, a prince: each is devout differently. He compares it to bees, which take honey from flowers without spoiling them. Real devotion, he says, makes your work and your home better, not worse. Third, gentleness with yourself. He warns against getting angry at yourself for your faults. When you fall, he says, don't rage. Pick yourself up gently, with sorrow but without fury, and begin again. Fourth, gentleness as strength. Tradition says Francis was hot-tempered by nature, and his calm was hard won. That's why his gentleness meant something: not weakness, but a temper held in a steady hand. Catholics hear his kind of gentleness in Jesus's words in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "learn of me, because I am meek, and humble of heart."
screen: `BISHOP OF GENEVA, LIVING IN ANNECY.` · `DEVOTION FOR EVERY KIND OF LIFE.` · `DON'T RAGE AT YOUR OWN FAULTS.` · `A TEMPER IN A STEADY HAND.` · then, large: `MEEK, AND HUMBLE OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one fault from this week and notice how you usually talk to yourself about it: a shout, a sigh, a long list. Now try it Francis's way: name it plainly, be sorry, then speak to yourself as you'd speak to a friend who made the same mistake, and begin again. If you pray, hand the fault to God; if not, simply set it down.
Philothea. The name Francis de Sales gave the reader of his book, one who loves God, written to show that devotion can fit any kind of life.
Your line: gentleness is strength. Every fall is a place to begin again. See you tomorrow.

864.title: Jane Frances de Chantal (1572–1641)
864.hook: a widowed mother who founded the Visitation sisters with Francis de Sales
864.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, and Visitation monasteries and schools carry on the community she founded with Francis de Sales; some parishes keep ministries for widows and the bereaved in her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis de Sales, who wrote to Philothea that every kind of life can be devout. Your line was gentleness is strength.

A hunting party in the French countryside. A shot goes wrong, and a nobleman is wounded by his own friend. Within days he's dead, and his young wife is a widow with small children and a grief that won't lift. For years she runs the household, cares for a difficult father-in-law, and prays without much comfort. Then, in Dijon, during Lent, she hears a bishop from Savoy preach, and something in her recognizes him. The widow is Jane Frances de Chantal.
screen: `A SHOT GOES WRONG.` → `A WIDOW WITH SMALL CHILDREN.` → `A BISHOP PREACHING IN DIJON.`

segments.voice: First, forgiveness. Tradition says Jane struggled a long time to forgive the man who shot her husband, and that in the end she met him, and later stood as godmother to his child. It didn't come quickly, which is part of why the story is told. Second, a friendship. Francis de Sales became her spiritual director, and their letters show a bishop and a widow each helping the other toward God. They wrote about prayer, her children, his work, and the quiet trust they shared. Some Catholics point to them as a picture of a holy friendship. Third, the Visitation. Together they founded a community of women called the Visitation, named for Mary's visit to her cousin Elizabeth in Luke's Gospel. It was meant for women the strict orders might turn away: widows, older women, women whose health couldn't take harsh fasting. At first the sisters went out to visit the sick and poor. Church authorities then required them to live enclosed, and the community adapted, with prayer at its center. Fourth, widows. Jane knew from the inside what the letter of James says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Religion clean and undefiled before God and the Father, is this: to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation." She had been the widow in that line. She spent the rest of her life making a home for others.
screen: `FORGIVING THE MAN WHO FIRED.` · `A BISHOP AND A WIDOW, AS FRIENDS.` · `THE VISITATION: MARY TO ELIZABETH.` · `SHE HAD BEEN THE WIDOW.` · then, large: `VISIT THE FATHERLESS AND WIDOWS.`

Your line: friends in god. Jane and Francis each helped the other toward God. That's eight hundred sixty-four days.

865.title: Vincent de Paul (1581–1660)
865.hook: a priest who organized charity across France
865.tomorrow: Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity
865.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Vincent de Paul, and parish groups of the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, named for him, visit people in need at home, run food pantries and thrift stores, and keep simple rules about how they serve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jane Frances de Chantal, the widow who forgave, and the Visitation she founded with Francis de Sales. Your line was friends in god.

Sunday morning in a small country parish. Just before Mass, someone tells the new priest about a family in a farmhouse outside town: everyone in it is sick, and nobody is looking after them. He mentions them in his sermon. That afternoon, it seems the whole parish walks out along the road with bread, soup and wine. It's beautiful. It's also chaos. Too much is arriving on one day, more than the family can use before it spoils, and next week they'll be alone again. The priest watches and thinks: love needs a plan. His name is Vincent de Paul.
screen: `A SICK FAMILY OUTSIDE TOWN.` → `THE WHOLE PARISH SHOWS UP.` → `LOVE NEEDS A PLAN.`

segments.voice: First, the young Vincent. Tradition, and Vincent's own later words, suggest that as a young priest he wanted a comfortable post and a good income. He found work in a rich household as tutor and chaplain, close to power. Second, the turn. Through that household he met the poor of the countryside: peasants dying with no one to hear their confession, parishes without real priests. He began preaching missions in the villages, and gathered priests to do it with him. They became the Congregation of the Mission, and their motto came from Luke's Gospel, where Jesus reads from Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." Third, the plan. After the whole parish showed up at the sick family's door, Vincent gathered the women of the town and wrote a simple rule: who goes on which day, what they bring, how they speak to the sick, how the money is kept. That small group, a Confraternity of Charity, became a model he spread to parish after parish. Fourth, the reach. He was chaplain to convicts chained to the oars of the king's galleys. He raised money from the wealthy for the hungry in war-torn regions. He worked with rich ladies and poor country girls alike. His gift wasn't only compassion; it was the clipboard. Charity done once, in a rush, he believed, can leave people worse off. Charity with a schedule, a budget and a rule can last.
screen: `A YOUNG PRIEST WHO WANTED COMFORT.` · `PREACHING TO THE POOR.` · `THE RULE: WHO, WHEN, WHAT.` · `GALLEYS, WAR, HUNGER.` · then, large: `TO PREACH THE GOSPEL TO THE POOR.`

segments.voice: Think of a need near you that keeps coming back, a neighbor who needs rides, a friend who's grieving, a shelter that runs short at month's end, and instead of one big gesture, picture a small plan: who could share it, which day, what exactly you'd bring. Let the plan get boring and specific; that's the point. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, simply let it take shape.
Confraternity. The group of women Vincent de Paul gathered in a parish with a simple rule for visiting the sick, a model he spread from town to town.
Your line: charity, organized. Love on a schedule outlasts love in a rush. Until tomorrow.

866.title: Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity
866.hook: sisters without a cloister: the streets and hospitals were their convent
866.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Louise de Marillac, and the Daughters of Charity still work in hospitals, schools and among the poor; some Catholic social workers and nurses look to her as a patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent de Paul, who saw a whole parish arrive on one day and wrote a rule for a Confraternity. Your line was charity, organized.

A young woman from the countryside arrives in Paris with a small bundle and one wish: to care for the poor and the sick. She has heard that a lady here trains girls for that work. The lady who takes her in is a widow of noble birth, anxious by temperament, who once wanted to be a nun and was turned away. Together they're about to build a community of women who serve God with no convent walls. Today, Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity.
screen: `A COUNTRY GIRL AT THE DOOR.` → `A WIDOW WHO WAS TURNED AWAY.` → `NO CONVENT WALLS.`

segments.voice: First, Louise. Born to a noble family but outside marriage, she grew up never quite belonging. She asked to enter a strict convent and was refused, partly for her health. She married, had a son, nursed her husband through a long illness, and was left a widow, troubled by doubt and worry. Second, Vincent. Vincent de Paul became her spiritual director and gave her work: visiting the charity groups he had started in the parishes, checking their accounts, encouraging the volunteers. She was good at it. She saw what the noble ladies couldn't do themselves: the daily, dirty, tiring care of the sick at home. Third, the Daughters. Country girls began coming to serve, and Louise took them into her own house to train them. That was the beginning of the Daughters of Charity. To keep them free for the streets, they weren't set up as an enclosed order. Vincent put it to them in words they remembered, paraphrased here: your convent is the houses of the sick, your cell a rented room, your chapel the parish church, your cloister the streets of the city. Fourth, the work. They nursed in hospitals, cared for abandoned babies, visited prisoners, taught poor girls. When a lawyer in Luke's Gospel asks who his neighbor is, Jesus tells the story of the Samaritan on the road and ends, in the Douay-Rheims: "Go, and do thou in like manner." The Daughters took that road as their cloister.
screen: `NEVER QUITE BELONGING.` · `VINCENT GIVES HER WORK.` · `COUNTRY GIRLS IN HER HOUSE.` · `HOSPITALS, BABIES, PRISONS.` · then, large: `GO, AND DO THOU IN LIKE MANNER.`

segments.voice: Think of the streets you'll walk or drive today and who is out there: someone asking for change at a corner, a person sleeping in a doorway, a delivery worker in the rain. Pick one, and ask what a small act of service might look like: a greeting, a bottle of water, a meal, a real look in the eye. If you pray, pray for that person by name or by face; if not, simply hold them, and plan the small act.
Louise. The widow Vincent de Paul trained to run his charity groups, who later gathered country girls into her own house to found the Daughters of Charity.
Your line: the street is the cloister. For the Daughters, holy ground began at the front door. Day eight hundred sixty-six, done.

867.title: The Sacred Heart (1673–1675)
867.hook: Margaret Mary Alacoque sees the heart of Christ burning with love
867.howItsDone: Catholics keep images of the Sacred Heart in homes and churches, some consecrate their families to it, parishes keep first Friday devotions, and the Church keeps the Solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Louise de Marillac and the Daughters of Charity, whose convent was the city. Your line was the street is the cloister.

A chapel in Paray-le-Monial, a small town in France. A nun of the Visitation, the order founded by Francis de Sales and Jane Frances de Chantal, kneels before the Blessed Sacrament. Her name is Margaret Mary Alacoque. She later wrote that Jesus showed her his heart: burning with flames, ringed with thorns, a small cross rising from it. She wrote that he spoke of a heart that loved people so much and received so little love in return. She told her superiors. They doubted her. Today, the heart she said she saw.
screen: `A CHAPEL IN PARAY-LE-MONIAL.` → `A HEART IN FLAMES.` → `HER SUPERIORS DOUBT HER.`

segments.voice: First, the picture. You may have seen it on a holy card, in a kitchen, above a church door: a heart on fire, thorns around it, a cross on top, often a wound, and Jesus pointing to it with his own hand. In the Bible the heart isn't only feelings. It's the whole inner person, where a life is decided. So for Catholics the Sacred Heart is Christ's love itself, human and divine, made visible. Second, it's older than the chapel. Catholics root it in John's Gospel, at the cross. In the Douay-Rheims: "one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side, and immediately there came out blood and water." An opened side; a heart left open. Third, the nun who wasn't believed, until a Jesuit, Claude de la Colombière, was sent to the convent as confessor. He listened, came to trust her, and encouraged her to write down what she had received. What she wrote asked for simple things: receiving communion on the first Friday of the month, keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and a feast day for the heart of Christ. Later, the Church made that feast its own. Fourth, the fire. In Luke's Gospel Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am come to cast fire on the earth; and what will I, but that it be kindled?" The flames answer that line. Some people find the statues too sweet. Catholics who keep the devotion say it isn't sweet at all: it's a love that keeps burning when refused.
screen: `A HEART ON FIRE, THORNS, A CROSS.` · `AN OPENED SIDE AT THE CROSS.` · `A JESUIT CONFESSOR BELIEVES HER.` · `FIRE CAST ON THE EARTH.` · then, large: `I AM COME TO CAST FIRE ON THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Look at an image of the Sacred Heart, at home, at church or on your phone, and let your eyes move slowly: the flames, the thorns, the cross, the wound, the hand that points to it. Then rest on one detail and stay there, without analyzing. If you pray, whisper his words from Luke, that it be kindled; if not, notice what that detail says to you.

868.title: Jansenism
868.hook: a strict movement kept people from communion; the Church later encouraged frequent communion
868.howItsDone: Catholics who are free of grave sin are encouraged to receive communion often, even daily, and before receiving they say together a form of the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, confessing they are not worthy and asking only for a word of healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sacred Heart, Cor Iesu: a love that keeps burning when refused. Your line was a heart on fire.

"Lord, I am not worthy." Just before communion at Mass, Catholics say a line borrowed from a centurion, an army officer, in the Gospel of Matthew. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Two halves. Now suppose someone took the first half so seriously they never reached the second. Suppose they decided the table was for people who had earned it, and stayed in the pew, waiting to be good enough. Today, a movement that pulled people that way.
screen: `LORD, I AM NOT WORTHY.` → `BUT ONLY SAY THE WORD.` → `STUCK ON THE FIRST HALF.`

segments.voice: First, a book. Cornelius Jansen, a bishop in Flanders, spent years studying Saint Augustine on grace. His long book on Augustine came out after his death, and the movement that followed took his name: Jansenism. It painted fallen human nature in very dark colors and was severe about who could be saved. Popes later condemned propositions drawn from the book. Second, a convent. The Cistercian nuns of Port-Royal, near Paris, became the movement's heart. Antoine Arnauld, a theologian close to them, wrote a book on frequent communion urging long preparation and real penance before receiving. The philosopher Blaise Pascal took their side in a public quarrel. These were serious, prayerful people who wanted reverence. Third, the cost. In practice, communion started to look like a reward for the nearly perfect. Some Catholics went a long time without receiving, afraid they would never be worthy. Fear of sin began to crowd out trust in mercy. Fourth, the Church's answer. Over time, Rome pushed the other way. Pope Pius X urged Catholics to receive often, even daily, and opened communion to young children. Pope Francis has written that the Eucharist is not a prize for the perfect but medicine and food for the weak. The Church still asks anyone aware of grave sin to go to confession first. That isn't Jansenism; it's a door, not a wall. Jesus said it plainly in Matthew: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill."
screen: `A BISHOP'S BOOK ON GRACE.` · `PORT-ROYAL: PREPARE, THEN WAIT.` · `COMMUNION AS A REWARD.` · `MEDICINE FOR THE WEAK.` · then, large: `THEY THAT ARE IN HEALTH NEED NOT A PHYSICIAN.`

segments.voice: If you receive communion, think of the next time you will, and answer any voice that says you haven't earned it with the whole of the centurion's line, both halves. If you don't, bring to mind one gift you felt you didn't deserve, a kindness, a second chance, a meal, and hold it like a gift, not a debt. Let it stay unearned.
Jansenism. A strict movement named for Bishop Cornelius Jansen, severe about grace and wary of frequent communion, which the Church came to resist.
Your line: not a reward. The week ran from honest martyrs and a gentle bishop to organized charity, sisters on the street, a heart on fire and an open table. Another week, done.
